items.title: 5,000-year-old skulls reveal a disturbing secret of ancient Egypt's first kings
items.summary: A 5,000-year-old mystery surrounding the tombs of Egypt’s first kings has taken a disturbing turn. Scientists reexamining 46 ancient skulls discovered evidence of potentially fatal head injuries in 18, suggesting that at least 39% of those studied may have been deliberately killed. The findings support a century-old theory that royal attendants were sacrificed when kings died, possibly to serve them in the afterlife.
items.t: 5,000-year-old skulls reveal a disturbing secret of ancient Egypt's first kings

items.title: Scientists capture electrons making seemingly impossible quantum jumps
items.summary: Scientists have captured electrons making seemingly impossible jumps across forbidden energy gaps in graphene, with some transitions occurring at a remarkable 100% probability. The breakthrough offers an unprecedented look at quantum behavior and could help unlock a new generation of ultrafast, light-controlled electronics.
items.t: Scientists capture electrons making seemingly impossible quantum jumps

items.title: In National Geographic’s “Expedition: Saving Our Seas,” it’s all hands on deck
items.summary: The documentary offers a window into scientists’ wonder and joy in their work as they discover new life forms in the depths of the Southern Ocean.
items.t: In National Geographic’s “Expedition: Saving Our Seas,” it’s all hands on deck

items.title: Noise pollution is reshaping the health and behaviour of animals everywhere
items.summary: There is almost nowhere on Earth free from disruptive human noise – but it's one of the easiest environmental problems to solve
items.t: Noise pollution is reshaping the health and behaviour of animals everywhere

items.title: Did El Niño cause an early breakdown in the polar vortex?
items.summary: The polar vortex winds have undergone an unprecedented weakening, which could bring cold weather to Europe. Some scientists suspect the record El Niño is to blame
items.t: Did El Niño cause an early breakdown in the polar vortex?

items.title: Researchers build the first ever quantum clock that uses sunlight
items.summary: Quantum clocks usually rely on advanced lasers and isolated atoms in the lab, but a new experiment showed that the same clock design can work with sunlight instead
items.t: Researchers build the first ever quantum clock that uses sunlight

items.title: The ‘hell chicken’ dinosaur was a real terror — to fruit
items.summary: Infernogallus – the ‘hell chicken’ dinosaur – evolved to eat a fruit-heavy diet. It may be the first evidence of fruit-eating adaptations among non-avian dinosaurs.
items.t: The ‘hell chicken’ dinosaur was a real terror — to fruit

items.title: Which science-fiction novels have been best at predicting the future?
items.summary: We’ve loved sci-fi at New Scientist for the past 70 years, but which novels got the future right? From Neuromancer to The Handmaid’s Tale, Emily H. Wilson picks the most prescient reads of the past seven decades
items.t: Which science-fiction novels have been best at predicting the future?

items.t: Can you pass our science quiz set by Nobel laureates?

items.title: Scientists discover a hidden danger of viral infections that vaccines may prevent
items.summary: A new study reveals that viral infections may leave behind hidden damage to the immune system long after symptoms disappear. Researchers found that mice recovering from an acute infection experienced lasting changes to their spleens and weakened immune responses, potentially leaving them more vulnerable to future threats. Surprisingly, prior vaccination completely prevented these harmful changes in the mouse model.
items.t: Scientists discover a hidden danger of viral infections that vaccines may prevent

items.title: Superheated magma could fuel towering lava fountains
items.summary: Why do some volcanoes erupt with spectacular lava fountains while others release lava more quietly? Scientists have discovered that a hidden effect of extreme heat inside magma may help explain the difference. Experiments revealed that superheated magma can delay crystal formation for more than eight hours, compared with just 20 minutes in magma that has not been superheated.
items.t: Superheated magma could fuel towering lava fountains

items.title: Dark energy may have flipped from negative to positive 9.5 billion years ago
items.summary: A mysterious force driving the expansion of the Universe may have undergone a dramatic reversal billions of years ago. Scientists exploring an overlooked branch of an alternative gravity theory discovered that dark energy could have switched from negative to positive roughly 9.5 billion years ago, potentially changing how we understand cosmic history.
items.t: Dark energy may have flipped from negative to positive 9.5 billion years ago

items.title: The Sun unleashed a monster storm. Earth may have made it worse
items.summary: The massive solar storm that illuminated skies worldwide in May 2024 has uncovered an unexpected twist: Earth's own atmosphere may have helped make the storm so powerful. Satellite measurements revealed that roughly 85% of the charged particles fueling the disturbance originated from Earth's upper atmosphere rather than the solar wind. Scientists also detected an extraordinary 40% weakening of Earth's magnetic field high above the planet.
items.t: The Sun unleashed a monster storm. Earth may have made it worse

items.title: Why we buy: 5 thinking errors companies exploit to make you shop
items.summary: As we near Black Friday, columnist David Robson explores the psychology behind our impulse to buy things – and how marketers take advantage of our brains to push us to purchase
items.t: Why we buy: 5 thinking errors companies exploit to make you shop

items.title: AI confirms a long-suspected limit on quantum computers’ advantages
items.summary: An AI-powered proof has rigorously shown that using quantum computers wouldn't have huge advantages for a whole class of mathematical problems, confirming a vastly influential conjecture
items.t: AI confirms a long-suspected limit on quantum computers’ advantages

items.summary:
Nothing really exists in isolation. Almost every part of our lives exists in a network. Consciousness arises from what neurons do together, life from what genes and proteins do together, society from what we do together. When researchers began mapping real-world networks in the 1990s – from the World Wide Web to Hollywood actors linked by films – they found that wildly different systems shared…

items.title: A robot has assembled a structure in space for the first time
items.summary: Autonomous in-orbit manufacturing will be key to any future space economy, and researchers have taken the first step with a robot building a radio antenna without astronaut assistance
items.t: A robot has assembled a structure in space for the first time

items.title: Economics, not climate summits, will dictate the net-zero transition
items.summary:
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham delivers his speech to the COP31 conference PA Images/Alamy 

The stench of hypocrisy is in the air at the COP31 summit in Turkey . UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wanted to show British leadership on climate action. Meanwhile, his government just green-lit the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea, which will emit up to 36 million tonnes of carbon dioxide without noticeably reducing energy prices, and it is considering approving the Rosebank oilfield and weakening its electric vehicle mandate.

The summit’s joint hosts, Turkey and Australia, are pushing for a clean energy revolution, but this week Turkey announced two new oilfields that would help boost production 30 per cent, while promising to double natural gas production. Australia has recently approved fossil fuel projects including a “climate bomb” coal mine extension that will emit enough carbon to kill an additional 15 million Great Barrier Reef coral colonies during every bleaching event. Meanwhile, the second biggest emitter, the US, is again boycotting the annual climate summit.

Read more 
 How incredibly simple tech can supercharge the race to net zero

While the world shaved more than 1°C off the warming trajectory after the 2015 Paris Agreement, “collective climate action has effectively stalled”, and current policies put the world on track for a catastrophic 2.7°C rise by 2100, according to Climate Action Tracker.

Advertisement 

But there is one piece of good news. The Global Carbon Budget also just announced that fossil fuel emissions are expected to slightly decrease…
items.t: Economics, not climate summits, will dictate the net-zero transition

items.title: Pink noise played during sleep shows promise for Alzheimer’s memory loss
items.summary: There is some evidence that pink noise signals can boost the brain's ability to clear out waste products. Now there are some indications that this might improve memory performance in people with Alzheimer's
items.t: Pink noise played during sleep shows promise for Alzheimer’s memory loss

items.title: A New Era for the Dawn of Life
items.summary: Creative, interdisciplinary, and bold, the study of the origins of life has entered a new age. Welcome to Quanta Magazine’s special series on the origins of life. The post A New Era for the Dawn of Life first appeared on Quanta Magazine
items.t: A New Era for the Dawn of Life

items.title: The brain’s fear center moonlights as the save button for memories
items.summary: What determines which moments are remembered? The amygdala, typically associated with regulating fear and aggression, may play a major role
items.t: The brain’s fear center moonlights as the save button for memories

items.title: The Evolving Story of How Chemistry Became Biology
items.summary:
Around 4.6 billion years ago, some 9 billion years after the birth of the universe, a cloud of gas and dust collapsed into the familiar blinding ball in our sky. Scraps of leftover material collided and accreted into the planets of the solar system, including our own. For the next few hundred million years, Earth was a hellish, molten landscape bombarded by meteorites. As it started to cool…

Source
items.t: The Evolving Story of How Chemistry Became Biology

items.title: Europe’s Hera mission is ready to double down on asteroid science
items.summary: Europe’s Hera spacecraft is just beginning its exploration of the binary asteroid Didymos in a mission that’s tantalizing scientists on two fronts.
items.t: Europe’s Hera mission is ready to double down on asteroid science

items.title: Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover
items.summary: Crows may be even smarter than we thought, and their brains are astonishingly fast. Researchers at the University of Tübingen discovered that crows can make visual decisions twice as quickly as humans and monkeys, taking just 235 milliseconds on average to identify the direction of moving dots while maintaining remarkable accuracy.
items.t: Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover

items.title: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again
items.summary: Scientists have developed an AI-powered approach that makes experimental bionic vision technology more precise, helping predict the flashes and shapes of light perceived by a blind man with a brain implant. By learning how an individual's brain responds to electrical stimulation, the technology could bring researchers closer to restoring some degree of sight to people with blindness.
items.t: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again

items.title: NASA’s Perseverance confirms a key ingredient for life hidden in ancient Mars rocks
items.summary: NASA's Perseverance rover has confirmed complex organic carbon just beneath the surface of ancient Martian rocks, raising intriguing questions about the Red Planet's potential to have supported life. The remarkable preservation of these compounds, along with similar discoveries thousands of miles away, suggests the building blocks of life may once have been widespread across Mars.
items.t: NASA’s Perseverance confirms a key ingredient for life hidden in ancient Mars rocks

items.title: A new treasure map reveals where Earth's lost prehistoric life may be hiding
items.summary: A sweeping analysis of 540 million years of marine fossils has revealed surprising gaps in our understanding of Earth's ancient life. Scientists discovered that some of the greatest opportunities for finding previously unknown species lie in relatively recent geological periods, rather than the distant past. By mapping unexplored fossil-rich regions around the world, researchers have created a powerful tool to guide future excavations.
items.t: A new treasure map reveals where Earth's lost prehistoric life may be hiding

items.title: A butterfly that fooled scientists for 200 years finally reveals its secrets
items.summary: Researchers have discovered that a familiar tropical butterfly actually belongs to three nearly identical species, including one previously unknown to science. Hidden ultraviolet wing patterns and DNA differences revealed the truth, leaving scientists puzzled about how the butterflies remain genetically separate despite living side by side.
items.t: A butterfly that fooled scientists for 200 years finally reveals its secrets

items.title: Earth's fiery birth may have created hundreds of oceans' worth of water
items.summary: Earth's water may have been born in the planet's fiery atmosphere rather than delivered by icy comets or asteroids. Scientists discovered that rocky pebbles reacting with hydrogen under extreme heat can produce water in minutes, potentially generating hundreds of oceans' worth during Earth's formation. The findings suggest that water may be a natural part of how rocky planets form, rather than something that must arrive from space.
items.t: Earth's fiery birth may have created hundreds of oceans' worth of water

items.title: A massive new simulation reveals how the universe emerged from darkness
items.summary: A groundbreaking new supercomputer simulation is revealing how the universe escaped its cosmic dark age and transformed into a cosmos filled with stars and galaxies. Called Lumina, it recreates 2 billion years of early cosmic history across a region 1.6 billion light-years wide, capturing extraordinary details that previous simulations could not.
items.t: A massive new simulation reveals how the universe emerged from darkness

items.title: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe discovers a hidden pattern in the Sun’s chaotic magnetic fields
items.summary: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe has revealed a surprising secret hidden within the chaos of space: turbulent magnetic fields reverse their direction of rotation when examined at extremely small scales. The discovery exposes an unexpected pattern in solar wind turbulence that could help scientists better understand solar activity and predict geomagnetic storms.
items.t: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe discovers a hidden pattern in the Sun’s chaotic magnetic fields

items.title: Scientists discover that necks didn't evolve for the reason we thought
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the first animals to venture onto land nearly 380 million years ago had surprisingly stiff necks, overturning a long-standing theory about evolution. Rather than evolving to help animals turn their heads, necks may have emerged as part of the anatomical changes that allowed them to move using their front limbs.
items.t: Scientists discover that necks didn't evolve for the reason we thought

items.title: Stone Age children left fingerprints on ancient art projects
items.summary: Natufian hunter-gatherers may have shown their kids how to sculpt clay, sets of preserved fingerprints suggest.
items.t: Stone Age children left fingerprints on ancient art projects

items.title: This magic mushroom can kill
items.summary: Researchers in Florida unearthed a “dark magic mushroom” that boasts a combination of hallucinogenic and poisonous traits.
items.t: This magic mushroom can kill

items.title: How a Metabolic Spark Could Have Jump-Started Life
items.summary:
For well over 4 billion years, the fire of metabolism has powered the engines of life. The ability of cells to gather, transform, and harness chemical energy from their surroundings is the central force driving the dizzyingly complex network of chemical reactions that sustains living things. Metabolism is so crucial to life that some researchers believe that these reactions could have helped…

Source
items.t: How a Metabolic Spark Could Have Jump-Started Life

items.title: The mystery of how hair knows where to grow may finally be solved
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the intricate patterns of hair follicles on mammals may arise from a remarkably simple process involving cells following chemical signals. The findings challenge a long-standing theory and reveal how nature can create complex biological patterns without a detailed blueprint.
items.t: The mystery of how hair knows where to grow may finally be solved

items.title: NASA reveals Earth's ozone hole has grown to a size not seen in a decade
items.summary: The Antarctic ozone hole expanded to its seventh-largest size on record in 2026, driven by unusual weather conditions that pushed it close to its historic maximum. Scientists say international restrictions on ozone-destroying chemicals prevented even greater damage, and Earth's protective ozone layer is still recovering.
items.t: NASA reveals Earth's ozone hole has grown to a size not seen in a decade

items.title: Light is hard to block from every direction. This physicist found a way
items.summary: Physicist Stefano Martiniani uses a computer algorithm to design new materials that could help advance light-based computers.
items.t: Light is hard to block from every direction. This physicist found a way

items.title: Scientists uncover a 192-year-old mystery hidden in a mangled silver coin
items.summary: A bizarrely deformed 1834 British silver coin found at a car boot sale may preserve evidence of a rare minting accident nearly 200 years ago. Advanced 3D scans and microscopic analysis revealed unusual metal distortions suggesting the coin was crushed under extreme pressure, potentially during its original production.
items.t: Scientists uncover a 192-year-old mystery hidden in a mangled silver coin

items.title: Where are all the males? Ancient human fossils reveal a startling mystery
items.summary: A remarkable discovery in a South African cave suggests that an extinct human relative may have created an all-female burial site more than 240,000 years ago. Scientists analyzed ancient proteins preserved in Homo naledi teeth and found no male-specific markers among at least 20 individuals, potentially solving a mystery that has puzzled researchers for over a decade.
items.t: Where are all the males? Ancient human fossils reveal a startling mystery

items.title: Scientists discover a giant 66-pound rodent that lived 34 million years ago
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered fossils of a giant rodent that lived in Thailand 34 million years ago, revealing that enormous rodents evolved much earlier than previously thought. Named Yakamys sirindhornae, the ancient animal may have weighed around 66 pounds, roughly twice as much as other known rodents of its time.
items.t: Scientists discover a giant 66-pound rodent that lived 34 million years ago

items.title: 237-million-year-old fossils reveal a bizarre armored sea amphibian
items.summary: A bizarre, heavily armored amphibian roamed the oceans 237 million years ago, despite the fact that modern amphibians cannot survive entirely in saltwater. Discovered in China, the giant salamander-sized creature may be the first known amphibian to have adapted to a fully marine existence.
items.t: 237-million-year-old fossils reveal a bizarre armored sea amphibian

items.title: The Case for a Bubble at Life’s Start
items.summary:
At its core, every cell is just a bubble of chemistry sealed inside a membrane. In modern cells, that chemistry is extraordinarily complex, orchestrating some 1 billion reactions per second. Likewise, its container, the lipid membrane, is built and maintained by elaborate biochemical mechanisms. But even the much simpler first cells would have needed a bubble too. Without a physical boundary…

Source
items.t: The Case for a Bubble at Life’s Start

items.title: Science to restore speech is moving fast. Here’s what’s next
items.summary: As neurotechnology aims to restore seamless speech to those who can no longer talk, what’s next for the science, and for the people it promises to help?
items.t: Science to restore speech is moving fast. Here’s what’s next

items.title: Toxic secrets are hiding in Arctic ice
items.summary: Toxic metals can harm human health. Arctic ice cores trace arsenic, lead and other heavy metals to historic mining and smelting in Montana.
items.t: Toxic secrets are hiding in Arctic ice

items.title: NASA’s CHAPEA Mars crew finally emerges after more than a year in isolation
items.summary: After more than a year of simulated life on Mars, four NASA volunteers have finally emerged from isolation, bringing a remarkable space exploration experiment to an end. Their experiences growing food, conserving resources, and overcoming Mars-like challenges could help NASA prepare for humanity's future on the Moon and Mars.
items.t: NASA’s CHAPEA Mars crew finally emerges after more than a year in isolation

items.title: Why heart attacks can still happen even when bad cholesterol is low
items.summary: Even when bad cholesterol is brought down to healthy levels, some people remain at risk of heart attacks, and scientists may have discovered why. Researchers identified two types of fat-carrying particles that appear to promote inflammation and damage blood vessels through mechanisms beyond cholesterol buildup.
items.t: Why heart attacks can still happen even when bad cholesterol is low

items.title: Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain
items.summary: A surprising discovery suggests that some early signs of Alzheimer’s disease may begin outside the brain. Using miniature laboratory systems made from human cells, scientists found that genetic mutations associated with inherited Alzheimer’s can disrupt nerve-to-muscle connections without any involvement from the brain or spinal cord. This could help explain why some patients experience changes in balance, walking, and coordination long before memory problems develop.
items.t: Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain

items.title: Fossil fuel emissions are down in 2026. Green energy isn’t the reason
items.summary: It's not quite a victory for humanity's transition to renewables. The dip is probably driven by high gas prices from the Iran war.
items.t: Fossil fuel emissions are down in 2026. Green energy isn’t the reason

items.title: Scientists finally discover why we learn to love bitter coffee
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a hidden gut-to-brain dopamine pathway that helps explain why bitter coffee and other initially unpleasant flavors can become favorites over time. The discovery reveals how the brain learns to crave certain foods and could eventually lead to new ways of reshaping eating habits and food preferences.
items.t: Scientists finally discover why we learn to love bitter coffee

items.title: Drugs like Ozempic may help reverse chronic kidney disease
items.summary: Scientists found that semaglutide, Ozempic’s key ingredient, repaired blood vessels, dampened inflammation and improved kidney function in patients.
items.t: Drugs like Ozempic may help reverse chronic kidney disease

items.title: A high-fiber diet may clear away plastic in the gut
items.summary: Research in mice shows that fiber may literally wrap around plastic particles to remove them from the gut.
items.t: A high-fiber diet may clear away plastic in the gut
